newsitem.title: USA: Fed expected to opt to hold interest rates steady.
newsitem.headline: Fed expected to opt to hold interest rates steady.

text.p: By Rich Miller, Economics Correspondent

The Federal Reserve is expected to hold interest rates steady into 1997 at a meeting on Wednesday and another in December, amid signs the see-saw U.S. economy is settling down to an even keel, analysts said.
"There really are no fire alarms ringing anywhere out there," explained Robert Dederick, economic consultant for Chicago-based Northern Trust Co.
Since trimming short-term rates in January, the U.S. central bank's policy-making Federal Open Market Committee has held rates unchanged as the economy has waxed and waned.
All 37 of Wall Street's premier companies surveyed by Reuters said they expect the FOMC to keep policy steady at its meeting on Wednesday and at another gathering on Dec. 17.
It was only seven weeks ago that many of the same firms were betting that the Fed would tighten credit to cool off an economy that seemed to be on the verge of over-heating.
But since then economic growth has slowed markedly, to an annualized rate of 2.2 percent in the third quarter from a rapid 4.7 percent pace in the second.
"While growth will pick up in the fourth quarter, it will remain at a subdued pace," said Chris Varvares, President of St. Louis-based Macroeconomic Advisers.

The slowdown is welcome news for the Fed because it means the economy is settling down to its long-run cruising speed of two to 2-1/2 percent growth per year -- a rate that could conceivably be sustained indefinitely without fanning inflation.

It has also proved to be good news for the financial markets. Wall Street stock prices soared to record levels last week and long-term bond yields fell as investors bet on a continuation of the 5-1/2-year-old expansion.
"Economic growth seems to be slowing down to potential," said a Fed source who declined to be identified.
But that does not mean that the central bank is about to let down its guard against inflation.
While growth has slowed, the economy is still operating at a "very high level," the Fed source said.
At 5.2 percent, the unemployment rate is hovering around a 7-1/2-year low and is at a level that in the past has presaged stepped-up wage demands from workers, and higher inflation.
So far, that does not seem to have happened. Inflation has remained well-contained and by some measures has actually declined in recent months.
Wages have shown some scattered signs of picking up, but employers' labour costs -- which include wages and benefits -- have been held down by slowing health care payments.
That has allowed companies to hold off from raising prices and has kept inflation down.

According to Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan, workers have been reluctant to press for big wage increases because they are worried about losing their jobs. But he has also said that this "worker anxiety" will ebb eventually and cannot be counted on to hold inflation in check forever.
The Fed's board recently reconfigured the computer model it uses to forecast the economy to take greater account of the impact of such expectations on growth and inflation.
But anti-inflation hawks at the Fed remain concerned that the economy is operating beyond its capacity and argue it is only a matter of time before price pressures intensify.
That is why some analysts expect the central bank to continue to lean in the direction of higher interest rates by adopting a so-called asymmetrical policy directive Wednesday.
That would mean it would be predisposed to increasing rates if need be to contain inflation.
Even some Clinton administration officials have begun to sound a bit cautious about the inflationary risks posed by an ever-tightening labour market.
"Clearly, there would be an element of unacceptable risk in aggresively pushing the unemployment rate ever lower," Treasury Department economist Joshua Gotbaum said recently.
